subject: biology
title: Enzymes
final_note: You worked through the key terms in Enzymes.

concepts.def: A biological catalyst, made of protein, that speeds up reactions in living things.
Part of the enzyme where the substrate fits and the reaction happens.
Substrate fits the enzyme's active site like a key in a lock — specific shapes.
Temperature at which an enzyme works fastest; above this it denatures.
pH at which an enzyme works fastest; e.g. pepsin in the stomach works at pH ~2.
Permanent change in enzyme's shape (often by heat or extreme pH) so it can't catalyse reactions.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Enzymes — a core area of GCSE Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Enzymes brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Enzymes.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: An enzyme stops working above its optimum temperature because:
options: it dissolves
its active site changes shape (denatures)
substrate runs out
it loses water

mcqs.q: Which is the best optimum pH for pepsin (in stomach)?
options: pH 2
pH 7
pH 9
pH 13

mcqs.q: What happens to an enzyme when it is denatured?
options: Its tertiary structure (3D shape) changes, particularly the active site, so it can no longer bind substrate effectively.
The enzyme has been completely broken into amino acids.
The enzyme has died because enzymes are alive.
Enzymes choose their substrate based on which one is most common in the cell.

mcqs.q: Why are enzymes specific to certain substrates?
options: The enzyme has been completely broken into amino acids.
Enzymes choose their substrate based on which one is most common in the cell.
Only substrates with complementary shape and chemistry to the active site can bind effectively.
Each enzyme can react with any substrate, but works fastest with one type.
Humans evolved from monkeys but chimps evolved from gorillas.
Humans evolved directly from chimpanzees, which is why chimps still exist as a less-evolved version.
No — humans and chimpanzees share a common ancestor; both have evolved from it.
Enzymes choose their substrate based on which one is most common in the cell.

mcqs.q: If an enzyme reaction takes 20 s at 25°C and 5 s at 35°C, how many times faster at 35°C?
options: 3 x
5 x
4 x
2 x

mcqs.q: A student measures how fast an enzyme breaks down starch at different temperatures. The rate rises to 40°C then falls sharply to near zero by 60°C. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Above the optimum the enzyme denatures, so the rate falls.
The enzyme works faster the hotter it gets, with no limit.
The enzyme is used up by 60°C.
Higher temperature increases the amount of substrate.

mcqs.q: An enzyme works best at pH 2. In which part of the body is it most likely to act?
options: The stomach
The mouth
The small intestine
The blood

mcqs.q: A student wants a fair test of the effect of temperature on an enzyme. Which variable must be kept the same?
options: pH of the solution
The temperature of the water bath
The reaction rate measured
The time at which the reaction starts to slow

mcqs.q: At very low substrate concentration, adding more substrate increases the reaction rate, but at high concentration the rate levels off. The best explanation is that:
options: At high concentration nearly all active sites are occupied.
The enzyme has denatured at high concentration.
The substrate has changed into a different molecule.
Temperature has fallen as substrate was added.
